Your phone rings. It's a number you don't know, from a city you've never been to. You pick up. You say: hello? ... Nothing. One second. Two. Three. Then a click, and the line goes dead.

Maybe nobody. Maybe a machine. And that silence is not the scam. It's the filter. Behind it sits a record. Americans told the Federal Trade Commission they lost fifteen point nine billion dollars to fraud in 2025. That's about forty-three point six million dollars a day. Today, we follow one call, from the silent ring to the empty bank account, and find out where the money goes. And by the end, you'll see why even that record is far too small.

Chapter one. The silent ring. Meet Ruth. She's made up, but her week is not unusual. She's retired, she's waiting for a holiday package, and her phone keeps ringing. Each time, the same thing. Hello. Silence. Click. The calls come at dinner. They come during her favorite show. Sometimes the screen shows a number from her own area code, so it looks like a neighbor. She answers anyway, because what if it's the delivery driver? What if it's her grandson?

Here's what that silence usually is. Many call centers use a machine called a predictive dialer. The Federal Trade Commission describes it plainly: it calls several people at once for every salesperson who is free. Whoever picks up first gets the salesperson. Everyone else is either hung up on, or left waiting in silence.

Chapter two. The machine in the back room. For real telemarketers, there are rules. Under the FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule, a call counts as abandoned if you answer and no live person comes on within two seconds of your hello. Two seconds. Legal callers may abandon no more than three percent of their calls in a campaign. They have to let the phone ring for fifteen seconds, or four rings. And when no one is free, they must play a message with the seller's name and phone number.
So the silence I keep hearing... breaks the rules?

For a real business, a long, empty silence can be a problem. But scammers don't follow the rules. To them, the dialer is a sorting machine. Some security experts warn that answering may tell the caller your number is live, and that a real person is on the other end. Nobody can prove what happens to one single number. But what happens next, to a lot of people, is in the FTC's data.

Chapter three. The second call. A few days later, Ruth gets a text. Then a call. A calm voice says it's her bank's fraud department. There's a problem with her account, and she has to act fast. This is the most common trick in the book. Imposter scams have been the number one reported scam in America for nine years in a row. In 2025, people filed more than one million imposter reports, and lost more than three and a half billion dollars. Nearly one in three of all fraud reports was an imposter.
If this already surprised you, hit subscribe. The next part gets worse.

The FTC says the costliest scams often start with a fake bank security alert. People reported losing nearly one billion dollars to business impersonators in 2025, and bank impersonators were the costliest of those. Government impersonators took about nine hundred twenty million dollars. Reports of fake government messages jumped forty percent, partly because of fake texts about unpaid tolls. And text messages were the most reported way scammers first made contact.

Chapter four. Moving the money. The voice tells Ruth her savings aren't safe where they are. They need to be moved. Right now. Don't hang up, the voice says. And don't tell anyone at the branch. Ruth's hands are shaking. She wants to do the right thing. This is where the money actually leaves. In the FTC's data, the payment methods with the highest losses were bank payments, then cryptocurrency.

And the biggest losses didn't come from fake bank calls at all. They came from investment scams. More than seven point nine billion dollars, about half of everything Americans reported losing in 2025. The average victim of an investment scam lost more than ten thousand dollars. And the contact method with the highest losses wasn't the phone. It was social media, with more than two billion dollars.
Wait... so the phone call is just the door?
Pretty much. The silent call checks who picks up. The text, or the second call, builds the story. And the transfer is where the money disappears.

Chapter five. The fifteen point nine billion dollar ledger. Put every report together, and 2025 looks like this. Three million fraud reports. Fifteen point nine billion dollars lost. That's about twenty-five percent more than 2024, when two point six million reports added up to more than twelve billion. Losses have gone up every year for six years: more than six billion in 2021, about nine billion in 2022, more than ten billion in 2023. Since 2020, they're up nearly four hundred thirty percent. The FTC says a big driver is more people reporting losses of a hundred thousand dollars or more.

Here's the twist. That record is only the part people reported. One study the FTC cites found that only four point eight percent of mass-market fraud victims complained to the Better Business Bureau or a government agency. So the FTC tried to estimate the real cost, including fraud nobody reported. For 2024 alone, it could be as high as one hundred ninety-five point nine billion dollars.
A hundred ninety-five billion?! That's more than ten times what people reported!

Chapter six. Never ever. So, back to that silent call. The silence itself took nothing from Ruth. It was a machine, sorting phone numbers. The money was lost later: in the second call, the text, the urgent transfer. That's why the FTC and its partners run a campaign called Never Ever, about the things real businesses and government agencies will never ask you to do. And this week, with holiday shopping in full swing, the FTC put out new alerts about grandkid scams and fake holiday search results.
Fifteen point nine billion dollars, reported. Maybe far more, unreported. And so much of it starts with three little words. Hello? Anyone there?
